title: Year 9 Chemistry school-style chromatography and Rf questions

questions.prompt: School-style data question: use Figure A. Calculate the Rf value for food colour C. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

feedback.short: Rf = distance travelled by dye ÷ distance travelled by solvent front.

questions.hint: Use the centre of the C spot and divide its distance by the solvent-front distance.

questions.prompt: School-style data question: use Figure A. Which food colour in the reference table could be food colour C?

feedback.short: Match the calculated Rf with the reference Rf measured under the same solvent conditions.

questions.hint: Calculate C first, then compare with the final column of the table.

questions.prompt: School-style data question: use Figure B. Which known food colour is the best match for the unknown sample X?

feedback.short: The unknown has an Rf of about 0.61, matching Carmoisine in this reference set.

questions.hint: Work out 44 ÷ 72 and compare the result with the reference table.

questions.prompt: School-style data question: use Figure B. Calculate the Rf value for sample X to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Divide the distance moved by the sample by the solvent-front distance.

questions.prompt: Use Figure C. The Rf value for dye D is missing from the table. Calculate it.
questions.hint: Use the two distances in D's row.

questions.prompt: Use Figure C. Which dye travelled the greatest proportion of the distance travelled by the solvent front?

feedback.short: The greatest proportion corresponds to the largest Rf value.

questions.hint: Compare the Rf values rather than the raw distances alone.

questions.prompt: Use Figure D. Which reference dyes are present in the unknown mixture U?

feedback.short: Match spots at the same horizontal height / same Rf under the same conditions.

questions.hint: Compare each U spot with the reference lanes at the same height.

questions.prompt: Use Figure D. What evidence shows that U is a mixture rather than a pure dye?

accepted: It produces more than one spot

feedback.short: A pure substance gives one spot under these conditions; a mixture gives multiple spots.

questions.hint: Count how many distinct spots appear in the U lane.

questions.prompt: Use Figure E. Why should Rf values measured in water not be directly compared with Rf values measured in ethanol to identify a dye?

accepted: Rf depends on the solvent used

feedback.short: Rf is condition-dependent, especially on the solvent and stationary phase.

questions.hint: The same dye can move by a different proportion in a different solvent.

questions.prompt: Use Figure E. Which solvent gives the better separation of the three dyes?
options: It cannot be judged from a chromatogram

feedback.short: Better separation means the spots are further apart and easier to distinguish.

questions.hint: Look for the chromatogram where the spots overlap least.

questions.prompt: Use Figure F. From which part of a chromatography spot should the distance travelled be measured?
options: The top edge of the spot
The bottom edge of the spot
The widest edge of the spot

feedback.short: Chromatography distances are measured from the start line to the centre of the spot.

questions.hint: Use a consistent reference point for spots of different sizes.

questions.prompt: Use Figure F. The centre of the blue spot is 32 mm from the start line and the solvent front is 64 mm from the start line. Calculate Rf.
questions.hint: Both distances are measured from the same start line.

questions.prompt: Use Figure G. Which two reference colours definitely match components of the black sample?

feedback.short: Matching components appear at the same height when run together under the same conditions.

questions.hint: Trace horizontal lines from the black sample spots across to the reference lanes.

questions.prompt: Use Figure G. What is the minimum number of components shown in the black sample?

feedback.short: Each distinct spot represents at least one component.

questions.hint: Count the distinct spots in the black lane.

questions.prompt: Use Figure H. What should the student change before starting the chromatography experiment?
options: Lower the solvent level so it is below the sample spots
Move the solvent above the sample spots
Draw the start line with a thicker pen
Make all sample spots touch each other

accepted: Lower the solvent level so it is below the sample spots

feedback.short: The samples must start above the solvent level so they do not dissolve straight into the solvent reservoir.

questions.hint: Look at the relative height of the solvent surface and the sample spots.

questions.prompt: Use Figure H. What could happen if the sample spots begin below the solvent level?

accepted: The samples may dissolve into the solvent and wash off the paper

feedback.short: The dyes can dissolve directly into the solvent reservoir instead of travelling up the paper with the solvent front.

questions.hint: Think about where the dye goes before capillary action can carry it up the paper.

questions.prompt: A dye moves 45 mm while the solvent front moves 75 mm. Calculate the Rf value.
questions.hint: Distance moved by dye goes on top of the fraction.

questions.prompt: Why must an unknown dye and reference dyes be compared using the same solvent?

accepted: Rf depends on the solvent, so the comparison must use the same conditions

feedback.short: A reference Rf is useful only when the experimental conditions match.

questions.hint: Think about what would happen to the same dye in a different solvent.

questions.prompt: A reference dye has Rf = 0.72. In a new run the solvent front travels 50 mm. How far should that dye travel if conditions are unchanged?

feedback.short: distance moved by dye = Rf × solvent-front distance = 0.72 × 50 = 36 mm.

questions.hint: Rearrange the Rf equation to find distance moved by dye.

questions.prompt: A student says, 'The unknown must be Carmoisine because it looks red.' Why is this evidence not sufficient?

accepted: Different dyes can have similar colours, so compare Rf values under the same conditions

feedback.short: Identity should be supported by chromatographic behaviour, not appearance alone.

questions.hint: Two different substances can appear to have a similar colour.

questions.prompt: Two dyes have the same Rf in ethanol but different Rf values when both are tested in water. What does this show?
options: The first Rf match alone does not prove they are the same substance
They must be the same dye
The water result should be ignored

accepted: The first Rf match alone does not prove they are the same substance

feedback.short: A single matching Rf is supporting evidence, not absolute proof of identity.

questions.hint: Identity should be consistent when the two samples are tested under matched conditions.

questions.prompt: A spot remains on the start line while the solvent front moves 65 mm. What is the Rf value of the spot?

feedback.short: The spot travelled 0 mm, so Rf = 0 ÷ 65 = 0.

questions.hint: Use zero as the distance travelled by the dye.

questions.prompt: A spot reaches exactly the solvent front. What is its Rf value?

feedback.short: The dye and solvent front travelled the same distance, so the ratio is 1.

questions.hint: A number divided by itself equals 1.

questions.prompt: Why does an Rf value have no unit?
options: It is a ratio of two distances measured in the same unit
The solvent front has no distance
Rf is always a whole number

accepted: It is a ratio of two distances measured in the same unit

feedback.short: The distance units cancel when one distance is divided by another.

questions.hint: Think about mm ÷ mm.

questions.prompt: Why should the start line be drawn in pencil rather than ink?

accepted: Pencil graphite does not dissolve in the solvent, whereas ink may dissolve and interfere

feedback.short: A pen line can dissolve and produce extra coloured marks on the chromatogram.

questions.hint: The baseline itself must not travel with the solvent.

questions.prompt: Why should chromatography spots be made small and concentrated rather than very large?

accepted: Small concentrated spots separate more clearly and give more precise positions

feedback.short: Large spots can spread, overlap and make the centre difficult to measure.

questions.hint: Think about what happens if two broad spots spread into each other.

questions.prompt: A student repeats an Rf measurement three times and gets 0.58, 0.59 and 0.58. What does the close agreement mainly suggest?
options: The result must equal the literature value

feedback.short: Closely repeated values indicate good repeatability / precision, not necessarily accuracy.

questions.hint: Precision is about how close repeated measurements are to each other.

questions.prompt: An unknown gives one spot with Rf 0.52. A reference also gives one spot with Rf 0.52 in the same solvent. Which conclusion is most scientifically careful?
options: The results support that they may be the same dye, but further evidence could be used
The unknown must be a mixture

accepted: The results support that they may be the same dye, but further evidence could be used

feedback.short: A matching Rf under matched conditions is useful evidence, but one test alone is not absolute proof of identity.

questions.hint: Distinguish evidence that supports a conclusion from evidence that proves it beyond doubt.
